The question of when the first immigrants came to Hawaii depends on which group is being considered. The earliest settlers were Polynesian navigators: according to the National Park Service, Polynesians from the Marquesas Islands were the first humans to settle the Hawaiian Islands between 1000–1200 AD [d10], while history.com places this settlement at around the 7th century [d3], and Wikipedia's Ancient Hawaii article notes scholarly estimates ranging from 400–1100 CE, with a 2010 radiocarbon study suggesting as late as 1219–1266 [d9]. A genealogy timeline similarly places the first Pacific Islander arrivals between 300–700 AD [d6].

Regarding later immigrant waves, Chinese sailors arrived on fur trading ships as early as 1788–1789, with an estimated 46,000 Chinese coming to Hawai'i between 1850 and 1900 to work on plantations [d5, d6]. The first Japanese immigrants, known as Gannen Mono ("First Year of the Meiji Era People"), arrived in 1868—approximately 150 people landing in Honolulu [d4, d8]. The first major organized wave of Japanese immigrants, about 900 people, arrived on February 8, 1885 [d2]. Waves of permanent immigrants from Japan, China, and the Philippines followed to labor in the cane and pineapple fields [d1, d7].
